title: When Reconstruction Is Not Enough: Doubly Robust Counterfactual and Interventional Mediation Analysis with Learned Multimodal Representations

paper.title: When Reconstruction Is Not Enough: Doubly Robust Counterfactual and Interventional Mediation Analysis with Learned Multimodal Representations
paper.abstract: Abstract Learned representations of high-dimensional multimodal health records are increasingly used to adjust for confounding, yet they are usually trained to reconstruct the data rather than to preserve the information that causal identification requires. We study two families of estimands: counterfactual outcomes under alternative treatments, including phenotype-specific effects and patient-level counterfactual risk profiles of the kind digital twins provide, and interventional direct and indirect effects under exposure-induced intermediate confounding. We give conditions under which a representation preserves identification and show that interventional mediation is more demanding than counterfactual comparison. We prove that no training objective that depends only on the covariates, whether reconstruction, contrastive, or physics-informed, can certify that a representation is sufficient, and in a linear structural model we show that a representation can lose an arbitrarily small share of reconstruction accuracy yet induce arbitrarily large bias. We decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators into a first-order representation bias, which neither double robustness nor cross-fitting removes, and a second-order remainder of nuisance-estimation errors, so coverage deteriorates as the sample size grows when the representation is insufficient. We propose a workflow combining modality-specific variational autoencoders trained outside the estimation sample, cross-fitted doubly robust and one-step estimators, locked phenotypes, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, portable representations for external replication, and diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and sensitivity. In simulations, a representation that discarded a rare confounder gave interventional indirect-effect intervals with 2% coverage at n = 3,000 n=3,000 when the confounder was moderately strong, reconstruction loss did not identify the problem, and a simple predictive diagnostic flagged it in 100% of replicates.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Electronic health records, biobanks, and participant surveys now describe patients through many data types at once: diagnoses, medications, laboratory values, vital signs, social and behavioral measures, and genomes. Causal questions asked of these data, such as whether a treatment works better for some patients than for others, or how much of an exposure’s effect on a later outcome runs through an early intermediate change, require adjustment for confounding by many of these characteristics simultaneously. A common strategy is to compress the multimodal record into a low-dimensional representation, for example with modality-specific variational autoencoders (VAEs) ( Kingma and Welling, 2014 ) , and to use that representation as the adjustment set in downstream causal analyses ( Cao and Ma, 2026b ; Cao and Ma, 2026a ) . The appeal is practical: nuisance models with thousands of sparse, correlated, and partly missing features are hard to fit, whereas a handful of learned dimensions is easy to work with. The difficulty is that a VAE is trained to reconstruct its inputs. Nothing in that objective requires the representation to retain the information that identifies a causal effect, namely information about how the exposure was assigned, how intermediate variables respond, and how the outcome is generated. A variable can matter greatly for confounding while contributing little to reconstruction, for instance a rare diagnosis among hundreds of codes. More generally, good predictive performance does not by itself yield valid causal estimates ( Westreich et al., 2020 ; Naimi et al., 2023 ) . In related settings we found that learned components that predict or reconstruct well can still yield poor causal answers: low nuisance-function prediction error did not identify the better causal estimator ( Cao, 2026b ) ; learned exposure mappings with near-identical predictive accuracy implied different spillover effects ( Cao, 2026a ) ; and different representation-learning objectives recovered different latent structures from the same data ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . For conditional average treatment effects, Melnychuk et al. (2024) showed that low-dimensional representations can induce confounding bias and derived bounds for it. Mediation analysis is more demanding still. When an exposure affects a confounder of the mediator–outcome relation, natural direct and indirect effects are not identified, and interventional effects are used instead ( VanderWeele et al., 2014 ; Vansteelandt and Daniel, 2017 ) . Their identifying functional involves the exposure mechanism, the distribution of the intermediate confounder, the mediator distribution, and the outcome regression, and efficient estimators combine all of them ( Díaz et al., 2021 ; Díaz et al., 2024 ; Benkeser and Ran, 2021 ) . A representation must preserve the information needed by every one of these nuisance functions. Interventional effects also depend on the covariates used to define the random draw of the mediator, so an insufficient representation changes the target itself, not only the estimate. Representation learning for treatment effects is well developed ( Shalit et al., 2017 ; Louizos et al., 2017 ; Shi et al., 2019 ) , and recent work characterizes which information in a learned representation suffices for efficient adjustment ( Christgau and Hansen, 2024 ) . Deep-learning approaches to mediation include debiased semiparametric estimators ( Xu et al., 2022 ) , VAE-based models with hidden confounders ( Cheng et al., 2022 ) , VAEs for multi-dimensional and indirectly observed mediators ( Jiang and others, 2023 ) , and joint representations of covariates and mediators within cross-fitted estimators of natural effects ( Bo et al., 2026 ) . These approaches either target natural effects or assume that the learned representation is sufficient. To our knowledge, the consequences of representation insufficiency for interventional effects under intermediate confounding, and practical diagnostics for it, have not been studied. This paper makes six contributions. First, we give sufficiency conditions under which a learned representation preserves identification of counterfactual means and of interventional effects, and we show that the interventional conditions are strictly more demanding (Section 3.1 ). Second, we prove that no training objective that depends only on the covariates, including reconstruction, contrastive, and physics-informed objectives, can certify sufficiency (Section 3.1 ), and, for a linear structural model, we derive the bias of interventional indirect effects induced by an insufficient representation and show that no function of reconstruction error bounds it (Section 3.2 ). Third, we decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators that use a learned representation into a first-order representation bias and a second-order remainder, and we show that coverage deteriorates with sample size when the representation is insufficient (Section 3.3 ). Fourth, we describe a workflow that applies one representation to counterfactual treatment comparisons, locked phenotypes, interventional mediation, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, and portable external replication, including time-indexed multimodal records with a pre-exposure window (Section 4 ). Fifth, we propose diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and representation sensitivity, together with a rule for choosing the representation by nuisance loss rather than reconstruction loss (Section 5 ). Finally, we evaluate these methods in a simulation study with a tunable information-loss mechanism (Sections 6 and 7 ).

Under external training (R1), the encoders are trained on covariate data from individuals outside the analytic sample, for example other participants of the same biobank, and then held fixed. sections.heading: Time-indexed records.
sections.text: In many settings the multimodal record is a time series, for example continuous physiological monitoring, device and activity logs, or audio and video recordings of a clinical episode, and the exposure is defined at or after a time zero t 0 t_{0} , as in target-trial emulation ( Hernán and Robins, 2016 ) . The framework applies with W W replaced by the pre-exposure window W < t 0 W_{<t_{0}} : the encoders are trained, and the representation is computed, only from data recorded before t 0 t_{0} . Data recorded after t 0 t_{0} may reflect the exposure or its consequences. Including them in the representation conditions on post-exposure variables, can encode the exposure itself (diagnostic D2 in Section 5 ), and changes the estimand. Post-exposure variables that are affected by the exposure and confound the mediator–outcome relation enter the analysis as intermediate confounders Z Z , not through the representation. When an exposure accumulates over a window, for example as a count or a rate, the window and t 0 t_{0} should be fixed in advance, so that longer or more complex episodes do not receive larger exposure values merely because they last longer.

sections.heading: Mechanism-informed objectives.
sections.text: The VAE objective can be augmented with penalties that encode mechanistic knowledge, as in physics-informed neural networks ( Raissi et al., 2019 ) , in which a learned model is also required to satisfy a differential equation; we have used this approach to forecast urban air pollution from traffic and weather ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . Two kinds of mechanism should be distinguished. A mechanism that describes only the covariates, for example the dynamics of pretreatment physiological trajectories, yields an objective that still depends on the law of W W alone and is therefore subject to Proposition 2 : it may make the representation more accurate or more stable, but it cannot by itself make it sufficient. A mechanism that links the exposure, the mediator, and the outcome, for example an energy-balance model of how a change in energy intake under treatment translates into weight change over time ( Hall et al., 2011 ) , constrains the nuisance functions on which sufficiency depends and may therefore help. Because such an objective uses A A , M M , or Y Y , it falls under the rule below, and its benefit should be checked with diagnostic D1 rather than assumed. Representations whose training loss involves A A , Z Z , M M , or Y Y (supervised or semi-supervised objectives) use outcome information and are admissible only under regimes (R1) or (R2).

Interventional effects are defined relative to the covariates used to draw the mediator. Remark 2 (Reconstruction targets none of these conditions) . The VAE objective depends only on the marginal law of W W . All conditions in Definition 1 concern the conditional law of ( A , Z , M , Y ) (A,Z,M,Y) given W W . Two data-generating laws with the same distribution of W W therefore yield the same representation, while one may satisfy sufficiency and the other not. Proposition 2 makes this precise for every objective of this kind, and Section 3.2 makes it quantitative. Definition 2 (Covariate-only objective) . A training objective for a representation is covariate-only if, for every candidate ϕ \phi , its value depends on the data-generating law only through the marginal law of W W . Reconstruction objectives such as the evidence lower bound, contrastive objectives defined on W W , and physics-informed penalties that constrain only the dynamics of W W are covariate-only. Proposition 2 (No covariate-only objective certifies sufficiency) . Let W W take values in a standard Borel space, and let ϕ \phi be a representation such that W W is not almost surely a function of ϕ ⁡ ( W ) \phi(W) . Then there are three laws P 0 P_{0} , P 1 P_{1} , and P 2 P_{2} with the same marginal law of W W , each satisfying Assumption 1 , such that ϕ \phi is process-sufficient under P 0 P_{0} , ψ ϕ ​ ( 1 ) ≠ ψ W ​ ( 1 ) \psi_{\phi}(1)\neq\psi_{W}(1) under P 1 P_{1} , and IIE ϕ ≠ IIE W \mathrm{IIE}_{\phi}\neq\mathrm{IIE}_{W} under P 2 P_{2} . In particular, every covariate-only objective takes the same value at ϕ \phi under all three laws, so no such objective, and no rule that selects a representation by its value, can distinguish a sufficient representation from an insufficient one. The only representations that are sufficient under every law are those that retain all of the information in W W , and they provide no compression. Sufficiency therefore has to come from information about the exposure, mediator, and outcome mechanisms, either through the training objective (Section 2.4 ) or through diagnostics such as D1 (Section 5 ).

sections.heading: 4 Estimation workflow
sections.text: The workflow fits one representation and uses it for every causal estimand. Throughout, the sample is split once into a development part 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} , used to train encoders under regime (R1) or (R2), choose the representation, and derive phenotypes, and an estimation part 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} , used for cross-fitted estimation with everything learned on 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} held fixed. All observations of a patient, and of a cluster when observations are clustered, stay on one side of every split.

sections.heading: 4.1 Counterfactual comparisons of treatments
sections.text: With cross-fitted estimates μ ^ a \hat{\mu}_{a} and g ^ \hat{g} computed on ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}(W) , define the doubly robust pseudo-outcome ξ ^ i = μ ^ 1 ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) − μ ^ 0 ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) + A i − g ^ ​ ( 1 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) g ^ ​ ( 1 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) ​ g ^ ​ ( 0 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) ​ { Y i − μ ^ A i ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) } , ϕ ^ i = ϕ ^ ​ ( W i ) . \hat{\xi}_{i}=\hat{\mu}_{1}(\hat{\phi}_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{0}(\hat{\phi}_{i})+\frac{A_{i}-\hat{g}(1\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})}{\hat{g}(1\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})\,\hat{g}(0\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})}\big\{Y_{i}-\hat{\mu}_{A_{i}}(\hat{\phi}_{i})\big\},\qquad\hat{\phi}_{i}=\hat{\phi}(W_{i}). Its sample mean estimates the average effect, its mean within S = s S=s estimates τ ⁡ ( s ) \tau(s) for a locked phenotype, and its regression on ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} in a further split gives the doubly robust learner of the conditional effect function ( Kennedy, 2023 ) . Under Proposition 1 (a) and Theorem 1 , these estimators are consistent for the W W -adjusted targets when ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} is balancing or prognostic, which is a weaker requirement than in mediation. The counterfactual risk profile r ^ a ( f ) ​ ( ϕ ^ ) \hat{r}^{(f)}_{a}(\hat{\phi}) is the cross-fitted outcome model for failure mode f f in treatment arm a a , evaluated for every patient under every option, so that each patient receives a profile of predicted failure risks across treatments and the failure most likely under each option. Because the profile is a plug-in quantity without an augmentation term, we check it against doubly robust targets: within bins of predicted risk, the mean of r ^ a ( f ) \hat{r}^{(f)}_{a} is compared with the doubly robust estimate of ℙ ⁡ { Y ( f ) ​ ( a ) = 1 ∣ bin } \mathbb{P}\{Y^{(f)}(a)=1\mid\text{bin}\} , which gives a counterfactual calibration plot for each option. Failure modes are treated as separate binary outcomes; competing failures can be handled with a multinomial outcome model without changing the rest of the workflow. Remark 5 (Counterfactual risk profiles as digital twins) . A model that predicts each patient’s outcomes under every treatment option is what the clinical literature calls a digital twin ( Björnsson et al., 2020 ; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024 ) . The results above state when such a twin can be trusted. For comparisons between treatments, the representation must be balancing or prognostic (Proposition 1 (a)); if the twin is also used to explain why outcomes differ, through interventional mediation, it must satisfy the stronger conditions of Proposition 1 (b) or (c). The counterfactual calibration check above validates a twin’s predictions under each option, and landmark updating (Section 4.3 ) corresponds to updating the twin with new data, with the caveat that updated predictions condition on the treatment actually received and are therefore not counterfactual comparisons between options.

sections.heading: 4.2 Interventional mediation
sections.text: Interventional effects are estimated with the cross-fitted one-step estimator of Díaz et al. (2021) , using ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}(W) or ϕ ^ + ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}^{+}(W) in place of W W ; the 2024 correction to that paper applies ( Díaz et al., 2024 ) . We write the mediator density ratio in the efficient influence function through Bayes’ rule, so that it requires only the probabilities ℙ ⁡ ( A ∣ M , V ) \mathbb{P}(A\mid M,V) and ℙ ⁡ ( Z ∣ A , M , V ) \mathbb{P}(Z\mid A,M,V) rather than conditional densities (Appendix B ). We implement the estimator directly because regime (R2) uses a different covariate matrix in each fold; for adjustment sets that are common to all folds it can be compared with the medoutcon implementation ( Hejazi et al., 2022 ) , which accommodates a single binary intermediate confounder, and settings with several mediators or intermediate confounders can use the extension of Rudolph et al. (2024) , implemented in HDmediation . The implementation reproduces the true values exactly when the true nuisance functions are supplied, and remains unbiased when the outcome model or the exposure model is deliberately misspecified. Variances are estimated from the efficient influence function, with cluster-level score sums when observations are clustered. When Y Y is an incident event, follow-up begins after M M is measured so that the mediator precedes the outcome.

sections.heading: 4.3 Phenotypes
sections.text: A phenotype is a pretreatment grouping S = s ​ { ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) } S=s\{\hat{\phi}(W)\} derived on 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} , for example by linking the representation to observed response and failure modes, and then locked. Each phenotype is described by the features of W W that distinguish it, so that it can be recognized without running the model. Locking is what makes phenotype-specific inference valid: because S S is a fixed function when 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} is analyzed, τ ⁡ ( s ) \tau(s) and the phenotype-specific interventional effects θ ⁡ ( a , a ∗ , s ) = 𝔼 ⁡ { ∑ z ∫ b ​ q ​ p ¯ ​ 𝑑 m ∣ S = s } \theta(a,a^{*};s)=\mathbb{E}\{\sum_{z}\int b\,q\,\bar{p}\,dm\mid S=s\} are ordinary functionals, estimated by within-phenotype averages of the corresponding uncentered influence functions. Deriving and evaluating phenotypes on the same data would make S S data-dependent and the resulting intervals too narrow. The added value of the representation is assessed by comparing phenotype and outcome models built on ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} with models built on conventional clinical characteristics and with models using the same data without a learned representation. Phenotype assignments can be updated at later landmarks, such as six weeks or six months after treatment start, by adding early response to the model without changing the phenotype definitions ( van Houwelingen, 2007 ) . Updated assignments condition on the treatment actually received and on early response, so they are predictions for monitoring, not counterfactual comparisons between treatments.

sections.heading: 4.4 Select-then-confirm pathway analysis
sections.text: When many candidate exposure–mediator–outcome pathways are examined, as in latent-space mediation analyses with hundreds of combinations ( Cao and Ma, 2026b ) , ranking and inference on the same data inflate the selected effects. We therefore split 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} into a screening part and a confirmation part. On the screening part, each candidate interventional indirect effect is estimated, candidates are ranked by | IIE ^ j | / SE ^ j |\widehat{\mathrm{IIE}}_{j}|/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{j} , and the stability of each candidate is measured by its frequency among the top K K across bootstrap resamples. The top-ranked stable candidates are then re-estimated on the confirmation part, with a Holm adjustment over the selected set. Because the selected set depends on the screening data only, the confirmation estimates retain their usual asymptotic distribution conditionally on the selection. We describe this step as internal re-testing, not independent replication.

sections.heading: 4.5 Portable representations and external replication
sections.text: Data sources record different variables. A portable representation ϕ c \phi_{c} is trained on the variables W c W_{c} that all sources share, with a prespecified substitute for any variable that one source records differently, and is applied unchanged elsewhere. Portability has a checkable and an uncheckable part. The checkable part is whether restricting to W c W_{c} already loses information in the development source: the difference Δ port = Ψ ^ ​ ( ϕ ^ ) − Ψ ^ ​ ( ϕ ^ c ) \Delta_{\mathrm{port}}=\hat{\Psi}(\hat{\phi})-\hat{\Psi}(\hat{\phi}_{c}) , computed on the same estimation sample with a bootstrap interval, should be near zero. The uncheckable part is whether conditional exchangeability between populations holds given ϕ c \phi_{c} ( Pearl and Bareinboim, 2014 ; Dahabreh et al., 2020 ) . External replication then compares prespecified quantities between sources: phenotype prevalence, defining features, calibration and discrimination of each outcome model, and performance across age, sex, race and ethnicity, and other prespecified subgroups.

sections.heading: 5 Diagnostics
sections.text: Theorem 1 shows that the representation bias cannot be controlled by the estimator, so it has to be examined directly. We propose four diagnostics, all computed without access to the outcome of the estimation sample beyond what the nuisance models already use.

sections.heading: D1: Nuisance insufficiency.
sections.text: For each nuisance function required by the estimand ( g g and μ a \mu_{a} for counterfactual comparisons; g g , q q , the mediator model, and b b for mediation), compare the cross-validated loss of a model using ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} with that of the same learner using ( ϕ ^ , W ) (\hat{\phi},W) . Per-observation held-out loss differences give a mean improvement and a standard error. A clear improvement shows that ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} is not nuisance-sufficient for that function (Definition 1 ). The converse does not hold: no improvement is consistent with sufficiency but does not prove it, and the diagnostic cannot detect unmeasured confounding. When W W is too high-dimensional for the learner, a penalized learner on ( ϕ ^ , W ) (\hat{\phi},W) or on ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} plus the residuals of W W given ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} can be used.

sections.heading: D2: Exposure leakage and overlap.
sections.text: A representation of a rich health record may encode the exposure itself, for example when diagnoses, laboratory values, or medications that define the exposure are among its inputs. We report the cross-validated area under the curve for predicting A A from ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} , the distribution of g ^ ​ ( 1 ∣ ϕ ^ ) \hat{g}(1\mid\hat{\phi}) , and the share of observations with estimated propensities outside [ 0.025 , 0.975 ] [0.025,0.975] . An area near one signals a practical positivity violation; the remedy is to remove exposure-defining variables from the encoder inputs, with trimming as a sensitivity analysis.

sections.heading: D3: Representation sensitivity.
sections.text: We recompute every estimate across latent dimensions, KL weights, random seeds, and representation objectives (VAE, principal components, and a supervised alternative) and report the range. Different objectives can recover different structures from the same data ( Cao et al., 2026 ) ; conclusions that change across this range are fragile.

sections.heading: D4: Choosing the representation.
sections.text: Reconstruction loss is reported but not used to choose the representation for causal analysis (Proposition 2 and Corollary 1 ). Instead, on the development data, we choose the architecture, latent dimension, and KL weight that minimize the sum of standardized cross-validated losses of the nuisance functions that the estimand requires. This targets Definition 1 (b) directly, although it remains silent about confounders that are not in W W ; standard sensitivity analyses for unmeasured confounding of the exposure–outcome and mediator–outcome relations ( VanderWeele, 2015 ) are reported alongside.

sections.heading: 6 Simulation study
sections.text: The study is designed following the ADEMP structure ( Morris et al., 2019 ) ; results are reported in Section 7 .

sections.heading: Aims.
sections.text: (i) To quantify the bias, variance, and coverage of cross-fitted estimators of counterfactual and interventional effects that adjust for a learned representation, as the representation loses confounding information; (ii) to compare the three training regimes; (iii) to test whether reconstruction loss tracks bias (Corollary 1 ) and whether coverage deteriorates with sample size under insufficiency (Corollary 2 ); and (iv) to evaluate diagnostics D1–D4, phenotype-specific estimation, select-then-confirm analysis, and portable representations.

sections.heading: Methods.
sections.text: All methods use five-fold cross-fitting with the same folds and the same nuisance learners, namely logistic and linear regression for adjustment sets with at most 30 columns and cross-validated lasso otherwise, with outcome-type nuisances fitted separately in each exposure arm. They differ only in the adjustment set or in how it is learned: (M1) the oracle, which adjusts for ( U , R ) (U,R) ; (M2) the raw covariates, all 61 variables of W W ; (M3) a VAE with external training (R1), with latent dimension per modality in { 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 } \{1,2,4,8\} , chosen either by validation reconstruction loss or by the nuisance-loss rule D4; (M4) a VAE with fold-specific training (R2); (M5) a VAE with full-sample unsupervised training (R3); (M6) the VAE from (R1) plus key covariates, ϕ ^ + \hat{\phi}^{+} , with two laboratory variables and R R as the key covariates; (M7) principal components trained on the external sample; and (M8) the VAE from (R3) without cross-fitting of the nuisance models. sections.heading: Performance measures.

sections.heading: 8 Discussion
sections.text: Learned representations make high-dimensional, multimodal adjustment practical, but they move part of the identification problem into the representation. The central message of this paper is that the error this creates is first order. Cross-fitting and double robustness protect against slow estimation of nuisance functions given the representation; they do not protect against information the representation has discarded, and that bias does not shrink with sample size. Larger samples make it more visible, because intervals narrow around the wrong value. Three consequences for practice follow. First, the requirements depend on the estimand: comparing treatments requires a representation that is balancing or prognostic, whereas interventional mediation requires that the representation preserve the information used by the exposure, intermediate-confounder, mediator, and outcome models together. A representation validated for one purpose should not be assumed adequate for the other. Second, neither reconstruction quality nor any other covariate-only criterion, including physics-informed penalties on the covariates, is evidence of adequacy for causal analysis; representations should be chosen by the losses of the nuisance functions the estimand requires and checked with diagnostics such as D1–D3. Third, representations should be trained outside the estimation sample, either on external covariate data or within cross-fitting folds, and known strong confounders should be added to the representation rather than left to it. Phenotypes and selected pathways should be locked on data separate from the data used to estimate their effects. The work has limitations. All results assume no unmeasured confounding given W W ; the diagnostics detect predictive insufficiency of the representation relative to measured covariates, not confounding by unmeasured variables, and a non-significant diagnostic is not proof of sufficiency. The closed-form bias is derived for a linear Gaussian model; the decomposition in Theorem 1 is general but conditional on a representation trained independently of the estimation sample, and full-sample unsupervised training requires an additional stability condition. The mediation estimator uses a single binary intermediate confounder. Counterfactual risk profiles are plug-in quantities and inherit the calibration of the outcome models. Mechanism-informed objectives that link the exposure, mediator, and outcome, and digital twins built on them, may reduce representation bias; whether they do is an empirical question that the diagnostics proposed here can answer, and we leave it to future work. Finally, the simulation study uses one data-generating design, two sample sizes, and 200 replicates per setting; applications to obesity treatment, comparing response and failure across metabolic and bariatric surgery and glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist therapy and decomposing the role of early weight change, are reported separately.

We study two families of estimands: counterfactual outcomes under alternative treatments, including phenotype-specific effects and patient-level counterfactual risk profiles of the kind digital twins provide, and interventional direct and indirect effects under exposure-induced intermediate confounding. We give conditions under which a representation preserves identification and show that interventional mediation is more demanding than counterfactual comparison. We prove that no training objective that depends only on the covariates, whether reconstruction, contrastive, or physics-informed, can certify that a representation is sufficient, and in a linear structural model we show that a representation can lose an arbitrarily small share of reconstruction accuracy yet induce arbitrarily large bias. We decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators into a first-order representation bias, which neither double robustness nor cross-fitting removes, and a second-order remainder of nuisance-estimation errors, so coverage deteriorates as the sample size grows when the representation is insufficient. We propose a workflow combining modality-specific variational autoencoders trained outside the estimation sample, cross-fitted doubly robust and one-step estimators, locked phenotypes, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, portable representations for external replication, and diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and sensitivity. In simulations, a representation that discarded a rare confounder gave interventional indirect-effect intervals with 2% coverage at n = 3,000 n=3,000 when the confounder was moderately strong, reconstruction loss did not identify the problem, and a simple predictive diagnostic flagged it in 100% of replicates. Keywords: causal inference; interventional effects; intermediate confounding; mediation analysis; representation learning; variational autoencoder; insufficient representations; counterfactual prediction; double machine learning; physics-informed learning; digital twins 1 Introduction Electronic health records, biobanks, and participant surveys now describe patients through many data types at once: diagnoses, medications, laboratory values, vital signs, social and behavioral measures, and genomes. Causal questions asked of these data, such as whether a treatment works better for some patients than for others, or how much of an exposure’s effect on a later outcome runs through an early intermediate change, require adjustment for confounding by many of these characteristics simultaneously. A common strategy is to compress the multimodal record into a low-dimensional representation, for example with modality-specific variational autoencoders (VAEs) ( Kingma and Welling, 2014 ) , and to use that representation as the adjustment set in downstream causal analyses ( Cao and Ma, 2026b ; Cao and Ma, 2026a ) . The appeal is practical: nuisance models with thousands of sparse, correlated, and partly missing features are hard to fit, whereas a handful of learned dimensions is easy to work with. The difficulty is that a VAE is trained to reconstruct its inputs. Nothing in that objective requires the representation to retain the information that identifies a causal effect, namely information about how the exposure was assigned, how intermediate variables respond, and how the outcome is generated. A variable can matter greatly for confounding while contributing little to reconstruction, for instance a rare diagnosis among hundreds of codes. More generally, good predictive performance does not by itself yield valid causal estimates ( Westreich et al., 2020 ; Naimi et al., 2023 ) . In related settings we found that learned components that predict or reconstruct well can still yield poor causal answers: low nuisance-function prediction error did not identify the better causal estimator ( Cao, 2026b ) ; learned exposure mappings with near-identical predictive accuracy implied different spillover effects ( Cao, 2026a ) ; and different representation-learning objectives recovered different latent structures from the same data ( Cao et al., 2026 ) . For conditional average treatment effects, Melnychuk et al. (2024) showed that low-dimensional representations can induce confounding bias and derived bounds for it. Mediation analysis is more demanding still. When an exposure affects a confounder of the mediator–outcome relation, natural direct and indirect effects are not identified, and interventional effects are used instead ( VanderWeele et al., 2014 ; Vansteelandt and Daniel, 2017 ) . Their identifying functional involves the exposure mechanism, the distribution of the intermediate confounder, the mediator distribution, and the outcome regression, and efficient estimators combine all of them ( Díaz et al., 2021 ; Díaz et al., 2024 ; Benkeser and Ran, 2021 ) . A representation must preserve the information needed by every one of these nuisance functions. Interventional effects also depend on the covariates used to define the random draw of the mediator, so an insufficient representation changes the target itself, not only the estimate. Representation learning for treatment effects is well developed ( Shalit et al., 2017 ; Louizos et al., 2017 ; Shi et al., 2019 ) , and recent work characterizes which information in a learned representation suffices for efficient adjustment ( Christgau and Hansen, 2024 ) . Deep-learning approaches to mediation include debiased semiparametric estimators ( Xu et al., 2022 ) , VAE-based models with hidden confounders ( Cheng et al., 2022 ) , VAEs for multi-dimensional and indirectly observed mediators ( Jiang and others, 2023 ) , and joint representations of covariates and mediators within cross-fitted estimators of natural effects ( Bo et al., 2026 ) . These approaches either target natural effects or assume that the learned representation is sufficient. To our knowledge, the consequences of representation insufficiency for interventional effects under intermediate confounding, and practical diagnostics for it, have not been studied. This paper makes six contributions. First, we give sufficiency conditions under which a learned representation preserves identification of counterfactual means and of interventional effects, and we show that the interventional conditions are strictly more demanding (Section 3.1 ). Second, we prove that no training objective that depends only on the covariates, including reconstruction, contrastive, and physics-informed objectives, can certify sufficiency (Section 3.1 ), and, for a linear structural model, we derive the bias of interventional indirect effects induced by an insufficient representation and show that no function of reconstruction error bounds it (Section 3.2 ). Third, we decompose the error of cross-fitted doubly robust estimators that use a learned representation into a first-order representation bias and a second-order remainder, and we show that coverage deteriorates with sample size when the representation is insufficient (Section 3.3 ). Fourth, we describe a workflow that applies one representation to counterfactual treatment comparisons, locked phenotypes, interventional mediation, select-then-confirm pathway analysis, and portable external replication, including time-indexed multimodal records with a pre-exposure window (Section 4 ). Fifth, we propose diagnostics for representation insufficiency, exposure leakage, and representation sensitivity, together with a rule for choosing the representation by nuisance loss rather than reconstruction loss (Section 5 ). Because the representation is itself estimated, where it is trained matters. We distinguish three regimes. Under external training (R1), the encoders are trained on covariate data from individuals outside the analytic sample, for example other participants of the same biobank, and then held fixed. Under fold-specific training (R2), within K K -fold cross-fitting, the encoders for fold j j are trained on the covariates of the other folds, together with the nuisance models for fold j j . Under full-sample unsupervised training (R3), the encoders are trained on the covariates W 1 , … , W n W_{1},\ldots,W_{n} of the whole analytic sample, without using A A , Z Z , M M , or Y Y , and the nuisance models are then cross-fitted. Time-indexed records. In many settings the multimodal record is a time series, for example continuous physiological monitoring, device and activity logs, or audio and video recordings of a clinical episode, and the exposure is defined at or after a time zero t 0 t_{0} , as in target-trial emulation ( Hernán and Robins, 2016 ) . The framework applies with W W replaced by the pre-exposure window W < t 0 W_{<t_{0}} : the encoders are trained, and the representation is computed, only from data recorded before t 0 t_{0} . Data recorded after t 0 t_{0} may reflect the exposure or its consequences. Including them in the representation conditions on post-exposure variables, can encode the exposure itself (diagnostic D2 in Section 5 ), and changes the estimand. Post-exposure variables that are affected by the exposure and confound the mediator–outcome relation enter the analysis as intermediate confounders Z Z , not through the representation. When an exposure accumulates over a window, for example as a count or a rate, the window and t 0 t_{0} should be fixed in advance, so that longer or more complex episodes do not receive larger exposure values merely because they last longer. Mechanism-informed objectives. The VAE objective can be augmented with penalties that encode mechanistic knowledge, as in physics-informed neural networks ( Raissi et al., 2019 ) , in which a learned model is also required to satisfy a differential equation; we have used this approach to forecast urban air pollution from traffic and weather ( Cao et al., 2025 ) . Two kinds of mechanism should be distinguished. A mechanism that describes only the covariates, for example the dynamics of pretreatment physiological trajectories, yields an objective that still depends on the law of W W alone and is therefore subject to Proposition 2 : it may make the representation more accurate or more stable, but it cannot by itself make it sufficient. A mechanism that links the exposure, the mediator, and the outcome, for example an energy-balance model of how a change in energy intake under treatment translates into weight change over time ( Hall et al., 2011 ) , constrains the nuisance functions on which sufficiency depends and may therefore help. Because such an objective uses A A , M M , or Y Y , it falls under the rule below, and its benefit should be checked with diagnostic D1 rather than assumed. Representations whose training loss involves A A , Z Z , M M , or Y Y (supervised or semi-supervised objectives) use outcome information and are admissible only under regimes (R1) or (R2). 3 When does a learned representation preserve identification? 3.1 Sufficient representations Definition 1 (Sufficiency) . Throughout, the sample is split once into a development part 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} , used to train encoders under regime (R1) or (R2), choose the representation, and derive phenotypes, and an estimation part 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} , used for cross-fitted estimation with everything learned on 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} held fixed. All observations of a patient, and of a cluster when observations are clustered, stay on one side of every split. 4.1 Counterfactual comparisons of treatments With cross-fitted estimates μ ^ a \hat{\mu}_{a} and g ^ \hat{g} computed on ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}(W) , define the doubly robust pseudo-outcome ξ ^ i = μ ^ 1 ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) − μ ^ 0 ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) + A i − g ^ ​ ( 1 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) g ^ ​ ( 1 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) ​ g ^ ​ ( 0 ∣ ϕ ^ i ) ​ { Y i − μ ^ A i ​ ( ϕ ^ i ) } , ϕ ^ i = ϕ ^ ​ ( W i ) . \hat{\xi}_{i}=\hat{\mu}_{1}(\hat{\phi}_{i})-\hat{\mu}_{0}(\hat{\phi}_{i})+\frac{A_{i}-\hat{g}(1\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})}{\hat{g}(1\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})\,\hat{g}(0\mid\hat{\phi}_{i})}\big\{Y_{i}-\hat{\mu}_{A_{i}}(\hat{\phi}_{i})\big\},\qquad\hat{\phi}_{i}=\hat{\phi}(W_{i}). Because the profile is a plug-in quantity without an augmentation term, we check it against doubly robust targets: within bins of predicted risk, the mean of r ^ a ( f ) \hat{r}^{(f)}_{a} is compared with the doubly robust estimate of ℙ ⁡ { Y ( f ) ​ ( a ) = 1 ∣ bin } \mathbb{P}\{Y^{(f)}(a)=1\mid\text{bin}\} , which gives a counterfactual calibration plot for each option. Failure modes are treated as separate binary outcomes; competing failures can be handled with a multinomial outcome model without changing the rest of the workflow. Remark 5 (Counterfactual risk profiles as digital twins) . A model that predicts each patient’s outcomes under every treatment option is what the clinical literature calls a digital twin ( Björnsson et al., 2020 ; National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, 2024 ) . The results above state when such a twin can be trusted. For comparisons between treatments, the representation must be balancing or prognostic (Proposition 1 (a)); if the twin is also used to explain why outcomes differ, through interventional mediation, it must satisfy the stronger conditions of Proposition 1 (b) or (c). The counterfactual calibration check above validates a twin’s predictions under each option, and landmark updating (Section 4.3 ) corresponds to updating the twin with new data, with the caveat that updated predictions condition on the treatment actually received and are therefore not counterfactual comparisons between options. 4.2 Interventional mediation Interventional effects are estimated with the cross-fitted one-step estimator of Díaz et al. (2021) , using ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}(W) or ϕ ^ + ​ ( W ) \hat{\phi}^{+}(W) in place of W W ; the 2024 correction to that paper applies ( Díaz et al., 2024 ) . We write the mediator density ratio in the efficient influence function through Bayes’ rule, so that it requires only the probabilities ℙ ⁡ ( A ∣ M , V ) \mathbb{P}(A\mid M,V) and ℙ ⁡ ( Z ∣ A , M , V ) \mathbb{P}(Z\mid A,M,V) rather than conditional densities (Appendix B ). We implement the estimator directly because regime (R2) uses a different covariate matrix in each fold; for adjustment sets that are common to all folds it can be compared with the medoutcon implementation ( Hejazi et al., 2022 ) , which accommodates a single binary intermediate confounder, and settings with several mediators or intermediate confounders can use the extension of Rudolph et al. (2024) , implemented in HDmediation . The implementation reproduces the true values exactly when the true nuisance functions are supplied, and remains unbiased when the outcome model or the exposure model is deliberately misspecified. Variances are estimated from the efficient influence function, with cluster-level score sums when observations are clustered. When Y Y is an incident event, follow-up begins after M M is measured so that the mediator precedes the outcome. 4.3 Phenotypes A phenotype is a pretreatment grouping S = s ​ { ϕ ^ ​ ( W ) } S=s\{\hat{\phi}(W)\} derived on 𝒟 dev \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{dev}} , for example by linking the representation to observed response and failure modes, and then locked. Each phenotype is described by the features of W W that distinguish it, so that it can be recognized without running the model. Locking is what makes phenotype-specific inference valid: because S S is a fixed function when 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} is analyzed, τ ⁡ ( s ) \tau(s) and the phenotype-specific interventional effects θ ⁡ ( a , a ∗ , s ) = 𝔼 ⁡ { ∑ z ∫ b ​ q ​ p ¯ ​ 𝑑 m ∣ S = s } \theta(a,a^{*};s)=\mathbb{E}\{\sum_{z}\int b\,q\,\bar{p}\,dm\mid S=s\} are ordinary functionals, estimated by within-phenotype averages of the corresponding uncentered influence functions. Deriving and evaluating phenotypes on the same data would make S S data-dependent and the resulting intervals too narrow. The added value of the representation is assessed by comparing phenotype and outcome models built on ϕ ^ \hat{\phi} with models built on conventional clinical characteristics and with models using the same data without a learned representation. Phenotype assignments can be updated at later landmarks, such as six weeks or six months after treatment start, by adding early response to the model without changing the phenotype definitions ( van Houwelingen, 2007 ) . Updated assignments condition on the treatment actually received and on early response, so they are predictions for monitoring, not counterfactual comparisons between treatments. 4.4 Select-then-confirm pathway analysis When many candidate exposure–mediator–outcome pathways are examined, as in latent-space mediation analyses with hundreds of combinations ( Cao and Ma, 2026b ) , ranking and inference on the same data inflate the selected effects. We therefore split 𝒟 est \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{est}} into a screening part and a confirmation part. On the screening part, each candidate interventional indirect effect is estimated, candidates are ranked by | IIE ^ j | / SE ^ j |\widehat{\mathrm{IIE}}_{j}|/\widehat{\mathrm{SE}}_{j} , and the stability of each candidate is measured by its frequency among the top K K across bootstrap resamples. The top-ranked stable candidates are then re-estimated on the confirmation part, with a Holm adjustment over the selected set. Because the selected set depends on the screening data only, the confirmation estimates retain their usual asymptotic distribution conditionally on the selection. We describe this step as internal re-testing, not independent replication. 4.5 Portable representations and external replication Data sources record different variables. A portable representation ϕ c \phi_{c} is trained on the variables W c W_{c} that all sources share, with a prespecified substitute for any variable that one source records differently, and is applied unchanged elsewhere.
